transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-03
Start: 10:00 AM UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (AE), Priya Natarajan (SE) - Redwood; Maya Chen (Head of ML), Diego Rivera (Platform Eng), Liam O'Connor (CTO) - AstraHealth
Links referenced: benchmark spreadsheet (drive link), Redwood POC runbook (redwood.link/poc-runbook), VendorX baseline report (vendorx.link/report)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then Priya will walk through the benchmark results we ran this week vs the baseline provider.
[00:15] Maya: Hey Jordan, yeah hi, Maya here.
[00:18] Diego: Diego here.
[00:20] Liam: Liam on the call.
[00:22] Jordan: Great. Priya, you want to kick off?
[00:25] Priya: Yep, thanks. So high level, we ran the same workload you shared last week — the 1k request sample with mixed short and long prompts, 32k token budget, and concurrency sweeps from 1 up to 64 sim connections. We compared Redwood hosted config (with our recommended batching and KV prefix cache) vs VendorX baseline that you shared. Quick note, transcription may swap VendorX name sometimes in the logs but it's the baseline.
[00:48] Priya: On median latency p50 we see Redwood at ~45 ms per token vs VendorX 70 ms, p95 Redwood 120 ms vs VendorX 190 ms. For p99 Redwood is around 420 ms but that's for long-tail long-sequence requests where KV cache warmup and context window hits matter; VendorX p99 was ~600 ms in the same runs. Throughput (tokens/sec) at steady state we saw Redwood sustain ~18k tps on a 4-GPU dedicated pod vs VendorX's ~12k tps on their standard instance.
[01:25] Maya: Quick clarifying q — those numbers are with quantized weights?
[01:28] Priya: Good call. The initial runs were float16 on both sides to keep apples-to-apples. We later did a quantized run (8-bit) on Redwood dedicated and saw p50 down to ~35 ms and p99 improved to ~350 ms for the longer sequences; throughput jumped to ~24k tps. We didn't have an apples-to-apples quantized VendorX run because their stack doesn't support the same quantization level easily — they have their own optimizations but not the same 8-bit path.
[01:58] Diego: Are those measured at application-level latency or per-token server-side? We care about end-to-end response time to the client.
[02:04] Priya: These are server-side token generation latencies measured at the service boundary — so they don't include transit time over your VPC peering, which you saw in your earlier baseline. We did attach a simulated network latency of ~15-25 ms to approximate your region. End-to-end should be + that network delta.
[02:24] Liam: So for our production SLO we wanted p99 under 600 ms end-to-end at peak, is that still looking feasible?
[02:30] Priya: Yes, with Redwood dedicated + quantization + prefix/KV caching we can hit p99 ~350-450 ms server-side in most of the runs; add your 25 ms network and you're still comfortably under 600 ms. The nuance is for very long sequences with cold caches under high concurrency — the p99 can spike towards that threshold, so we recommended further tuning: warm prefix cache, sticky routing, and a slightly higher burst capacity.
[02:56] Maya: Can you say more about sticky routing?
[02:58] Priya: Sure — it's routing requests from a given session to the same worker to keep the KV cache warm. That reduces cold-start in the KV cache and avoids re-populating large context windows repeatedly. We were able to reduce repeated cache misses by ~40% in some of the microbenchmarks.
[03:20] Jordan: We also tried a fallback policy in the experiment — when a worker sees latency above threshold it routes to a lower-capacity model to preserve tail latency. That impacted cost but kept p99 bounded.
[03:34] Diego: Cost's a big concern. How does the cost per 1M tokens compare in these configs?
[03:38] Priya: So rough numbers from the POC: Redwood hosted standard float16 run is roughly 20% cheaper per token vs VendorX baseline at the same config. On dedicated with quantization and improved batching the unit cost drops further — approx 35% lower than VendorX in our estimate. These are ballpark because the exact pricing will depend on commit sizes and autoscaling behavior. We'll send a detailed cost sheet.
[04:03] Maya: Are those costs including the additional storage for KV cache and network egress?
[04:07] Priya: Egress not included in that per-token estimate; KV cache RAM is part of the instance cost and we've included that. If you plan cross-region traffic or heavy egress we'll add that as a separate line item.
[04:18] Liam: There was one run where VendorX had slightly better p95 for short prompts at very low concurrency — any idea why?
[04:24] Priya: Yes we noticed that. VendorX's node scheduler sometimes prioritizes very short runs in their single-threaded path which gives them an edge at tiny loads. But the moment you increase concurrency or add long sequences Redwood's continuous batching and multi-GPU kernel selections outperform. So it's a micro-optimization tradeoff.
[04:44] Diego: On the reliability front we saw VendorX had fewer transient timeouts in one of our spike tests. Did you see that?
[04:50] Priya: We saw a couple of transient spikes during one of our concurrency bursts — that was during cold-start of a new worker. We've proposed autoscaling with warm standby and pre-warmed checkpoints to reduce that. Also sticky routing helps. We can also add a short client-side retry with idempotency token to hide transient errors.
[05:10] Maya: Security question — any differences in audit logging and key management?
[05:14] Jordan: Redwood Private offers customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations in the Private deployment; for the hosted POC we used our standard KMS but can switch to bring-your-own-key if you want. Audit logs are enabled on request; we'll share the SOC2/ISO/pen test reports.
[05:29] Diego: Great, send those.
[05:31] Priya: We also ran an experiment with different batch sizes. At batch size 32 we saw better GPU utilization and lower cost but a slight increase in p50 for short prompts (~+8 ms). At batch size 8 p50 was lowest but throughput dropped. So it's that classic latency vs cost tradeoff.
[05:52] Maya: Is there an automatic suggestion engine for batching?
[05:55] Priya: Yes, Redwood Optimize will suggest batching and quantization profiles based on your observed traffic. We ran an offline suggestion and it recommended dynamic batching with a 12-48 range and stricter limits for sessions marked low-latency.
[06:12] Jordan: I want to highlight the quantized run numbers again — 8-bit gave a substantial throughput improvement. But we saw a tiny accuracy delta on extraction tasks (~0.6% on our eval set). Did you notice any QA differences, Maya?
[06:26] Maya: We ran a 500-sample eval set — some hallucination cases increased slightly but still within our tolerance. We'll share the eval results in the sheet.
[06:34] Priya: Perfect. On the long-tail p99 issue we propose three action items we already put in the sheet: 1) pre-warm large-context workers for scheduled peaks; 2) enable sticky routing; 3) run a dedicated quantized run on a 4-GPU reserved pool. Those reduce the tail significantly.
[06:50] Diego: About the dedicated pool, how fast can you spin that up? We may want to try the 4-GPU reserved for a week.
[06:55] Priya: We can spin up a temporary reserved pool within 48 hours for a POC test; for contractual reserved capacity we'd need a lead time of a week and a short agreement. For the test pool we can do ephemeral instances.
[07:07] Liam: Are there any blockers for running the quantized 4-GPU test in our VPC?
[07:11] Priya: We'll need your VPC peering details and an IAM role for the test accounts. Diego, you mentioned you'd provide that in the notes.
[07:18] Diego: Yes I'll add VPC peering CIDR and test creds to the ticket after this call.
[07:22] Maya: One more question — can Redwood replicate our exact baseline VendorX config to make sure we're comparing the same model version and tokenization?
[07:29] Priya: We attempted to replicate model family and tokenizer but VendorX had a slightly different tokenization and chunking behavior. We matched model size and prompt setup as closely as possible; we documented differences in the spreadsheet. If you can export a few tokenized traces we can reproduce them exactly.
[07:45] Jordan: On the compliance front, Jordan again — we'll share SOC2 audit and our data retention options. If you need an on-prem/private deployment we can scope that but it adds lead time.
[07:56] Liam: For procurement timeline — if the POC goes well we want to pilot in staging by end of May. Is that achievable?
[08:02] Priya: Yes, if we complete the dedicated quantized run and validate in VPC by mid-April, staging by end of May is realistic. We'll need sign-off on cost and security review though.
[08:12] Maya: For the next run, can you include a test that simulates our burst profile — we have sudden daily spikes at ~2k concurrent for 2-3 minutes.
[08:21] Priya: Absolutely — please drop that profile in the shared spreadsheet, we'll schedule the spike test on the dedicated pool.
[08:28] Diego: A small nit on the logs — some of the timestamps looked like local time vs UTC in the vendor logs; made correlation tricky. Can you standardize the export to ISO UTC?
[08:36] Jordan: Yes, we'll provide ISO8601 UTC exports for the raw logs.
[08:40] Priya: Cool. I'll recap the concrete next steps now.
[08:44] Priya: 1) We will share the detailed raw logs and the benchmark spreadsheet by Monday 2026-04-05. 2) We'll provision a temporary 4-GPU dedicated quantized pool and run the tau-sized 5k sample and the burst profile, aiming to complete by 2026-04-10. 3) Astra to provide VPC peering info and sample traffic distributions by 2026-04-07. 4) Redwood will send SOC2/ISO docs and a preliminary cost estimate for the dedicated config by 2026-04-06.
[09:07] Maya: Sounds good. Diego will upload the VPC details.
[09:10] Diego: Yep I'll post them right after this.
[09:12] Liam: Thanks, this was helpful. One ask — can you add a column in the sheet for our internal success criteria (p99 < 600 ms end-to-end, throughput >= 10k tps at peak)?
[09:22] Jordan: Will do. We'll add an acceptance criteria column and flag any runs that fall outside.
[09:26] Priya: Anything else before we close?
[09:29] Maya: Not from me.
[09:30] Diego: All good.
[09:31] Jordan: Alright thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the sheets and the provisioning details.
[09:35] Priya: Thanks all.

Recap / Meeting close at ~10:45 UTC

Notes about transcription: minor mis-hearings for VendorX brand, some timestamps approximate. Natural speech fillers kept (um, yeah, right).

Attachments to follow: benchmark_spreadsheet.csv (drive link), raw_server_logs.zip (s3 link), SOC2_summary.pdf (redwood.link/soc2)
